candidates.exact_span: As used in this document, references to State water quality standards and/or rules, regulations and/or management plans may mean the State of New Mexico and/or Tribal or both.
candidates.computation_change_reason: The phrase 'may mean the State of New Mexico and/or Tribal or both' leaves ambiguous whether applicable standards, rules, regulations, and management plans are NM-only, Tribal-only, or jointly applicable; different readings could change which numeric limits govern (A), which monitoring obligations attach to those standards (B), and how missing or conditional results are classified when the governing requirement set is unclear (C).

This defines a limit category used elsewhere in the permit; whether a reported measurement is compared against a WQBEL—and whether that comparison is an enforceable numeric compliance determination—depends on how WQBELs are interpreted relative to other limitation types.

WLA denotes allocation-derived limits; interpretation of whether a measurement must be compared to a WLA-based numeric limit (versus another allocation or limit basis) can change which enforceable limit is selected for compliance evaluation.

WET is a distinct parameter class with its own numeric endpoints and monitoring triggers; how 'whole effluent toxicity' is read can change whether WET results are subject to numeric limit comparison (A), whether WET monitoring was required under applicable conditions (B), and how absent or non-numeric WET evidence is categorized (C).

WQMP-referenced provisions may supply effluent limits or monitoring conditions; interpretation of whether a cited management plan imposes enforceable numeric limits or monitoring duties can change limit applicability (A) and obligation applicability (B).
